subject: barcodes
title: The Stripes That Beep
summary: How a few black stripes tell the store what you are buying, and why they came from lines in the sand.

keys.answer: The pattern of dark bars and white spaces. Dark bars soak up light and white spaces bounce it back.

cards.title: Go find some stripes
cards.text: Grab a cereal box, a juice box or a book. Somewhere on it is a patch of black stripes with numbers under it. Some stripes are thin and some are thick. What could a bunch of stripes be telling the store?

cards.question: What do you think the barcode on a can of soda holds?

options.text: A number that names that soda

cards.reveal: A number that names the product. The store's computer looks up the price for that number.

cards.title: Lines in the sand
cards.text: Long ago, an inventor named Joe Woodland wanted to speed up the grocery checkout. One day at a beach in Miami, he ran his fingers through the sand. He thought of Morse code, which uses dots and dashes. His lines in the sand gave him an idea: wide lines and thin lines could stand for information too.
cards.example: Morse code spells letters with short dots and long dashes. A barcode does the same job with thin and wide stripes.

cards.title: Light and dark
cards.text: A scanner shines light on the stripes. Dark bars soak up the light. White spaces bounce it back. A sensor feels the bright and dark flashes and measures how wide each stripe is. That pattern turns into a number.

why.q: Why are barcodes black stripes on white, and not gray on gray?
why.a: The scanner tells bars from spaces by how much light bounces back. Black soaks up light and white bounces it back, so the difference is easy to see.

cards.example: It is a bit like a flashlight on a fence. The boards and the gaps look different, so you could count them in the dark.

cards.title: A name tag, not a price tag
cards.text: The barcode is a number that names the product, like a name tag. The store keeps a list in its computer with that number and a price. When the cashier scans your soda, the computer looks up the price. It also takes one soda off the count of how many are left.

why.q: Why not just put the price in the barcode?
why.a: The store sets the price and keeps it in its own computer. So the store can change a price without changing the code on every can.

cards.example: Say the soda goes on sale. The store changes one number in its computer. The cans on the shelf stay the same.

cards.title: The first beep
cards.text: The first barcode scan in a store was on June 26, 1974, in Troy, Ohio. It was a pack of Juicy Fruit gum, and it rang up 67 cents. Today, barcodes get scanned about 6 billion times a day around the world.
cards.example: Barcodes are not just for food now. They help with library books and boarding passes, and even help hospitals keep track of newborn babies.

cards.question: Imagine your favorite store with no barcodes at all. What would be harder for the cashier? What would be harder for the people who fill the shelves?
nudges: How would the cashier know each price?
How would the store know when the gum is almost gone?

questions.q: How does a scanner tell a dark bar from a white space?

options.text: Dark bars soak up light, and white spaces bounce it back
options.why: Yes! The sensor feels which parts are bright and which are dark.

options.text: It feels bumps on the paper
options.why: Good guess, but barcodes are flat. The scanner uses light.
The beep comes after the scan. It means the scan worked.

options.text: Just the price in the store's computer
options.why: Right! The barcode only names the soda. The price lives in the computer.
No need. The barcode is a name tag, not a price tag.
The scanner stays the same. It just reads the number.

sources.title: The UPC
sources.supports: Joe Woodland at his grandfather's Miami apartment, a day at the beach, fingers through the sand, Morse code dots and dashes, wide and narrow lines; first UPC swipe June 26, 1974 at Marsh's Supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a 67-cent pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum; about 6 billion barcode swipes a day; barcodes on library books, boarding passes and used for tracking newborns.

sources.title: Barcode reader
sources.supports: The scanner's light reflects off the code; dark bars absorb light and white spaces reflect it; the sensor measures the widths of bars and spaces.

sources.title: What Is a GTIN?
sources.supports: The lemon-soda example: the brand gives the product its number, the store adds the price to its database, scanning looks up the price, and the count of units is updated.
